# A sort key belongs to a level, not to a whole entry

Both back-ends order an index level by level: the LaTeX index tool reads a
sort key inside each level of an entry, and the HTML index keys each node on
its own printed text. So a key written for a level has to apply to that level
wherever it appears — on its own, or above a sub-entry. Were a key instead
remembered against the whole entry that declared it, the same printed term
would file under two different keys depending on whether a sub-entry happened
to follow it, and an index would carry it twice, in two places, printed
identically.

The key is declared on the term alone, and the sub-entry written later must
inherit it: [The Hague]{.index entry="Hague, The" sort="Hague"} has a district
[Scheveningen]{.index entry="Hague, The!Scheveningen"}.

The other way round — the key declared where the term carries a sub-entry, and
the bare term written later:
[Alpha]{.index entry="Alpha!inner" sort="Zed"} and later plain
[Alpha]{.index entry="Alpha"}.

A key written for a level must not climb to the level above it. Only the
second level is redirected here, so the first keeps its own printed text:
[Beta]{.index entry="Beta!gamma" sort="!gkey"} and later plain
[Beta]{.index entry="Beta"}.

A level a declaring mark leaves alone must not shut out the mark that does
declare it. The first mark below writes nothing for its first level; the
second writes a key for exactly that level, and it is the second that must
win, because it is the only declaration either mark makes there:
[Ccc]{.index entry="Ccc!p" sort="!pk"} and later
[Ccc]{.index entry="Ccc" sort="Www"}.
